SK0290 The explicit Nullable<T> construction converts nothing

new int?(x) or new Nullable<int>(x) written where the position already imposes int?, so the constructor call performs the same conversion the language performs implicitly.

CategoryCleanup
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, safe
Language version floor—
Since2.0

Why

The implicit conversion from T to T? is that constructor call, written out. Spelling it makes a reader ask what the wrapper is for, and the answer where the target type is written is nothing.

Example

Instead of:

int? first = new int?(5);
int? Second() => new int?(Compute());
total = new Nullable<int>(count);

Write:

int? first = 5;
int? Second() => Compute();
total = count;

When it does not fire

⚠ Whether the wrapper converts nothing is a question about the position, and the semantic model cannot be asked it. GetSpeculativeTypeInfo at a position binds the operand as a standalone expression, so for new int?(5) the operand's ConvertedType comes back int in every context — including every context where the rewrite is correct. A guard built on it would withdraw every finding and look exactly like a rule with nothing to find, which is SK0234's recorded lesson (#128). The target type is therefore not inferred but read off the syntax, and the rule reports in a whitelist of written-type positions and nowhere else. ⚠ Four positions are covered: a declaration initializer under a written type, a return or expression body under a member whose return type is written, the right side of a simple assignment whose left side is exactly the nullable type, and an argument whose parameter is exactly the nullable type. ⚠ `var` is the trap the whitelist exists for: var x = new int?(5); types x as int? and var x = 5; types it as int, and GetTypeInfo on the var keyword answers int? for both — only the syntax separates them, so var is refused syntactically. ⚠ A lambda and an anonymous method stop the return-position walk: their target type comes from the delegate being converted to, not from anything written at the return, and climbing past them would read the enclosing method's promise instead. async and iterator members need no case of their own — an async member's written return type is Task<int?>, never int?, and an iterator cannot carry return expr; at all (CS1622). Operators, conversion operators and constructors end the walk without an answer rather than being guessed at. ⚠ The argument position is unsafe on the parameter's type alone. With void M(int x) and void M(int? x) both in scope, M(new int?(5)) calls the second and M(5) calls the first, so the call is rebuilt without the wrapper and rebound speculatively, and only an identical symbol counts; SpeculativeBinding.CanBindDetached is asked first, because a detached member binding makes the compiler throw inside the analyzer and an analyzer exception is AD0001 and therefore nothing at all in a report. ⚠ The operand's type must be exactly `T`. new int?(someByte) is refused: the constructor call is performing a numeric conversion as well, and asking for the identical type is how that question is never asked. ⚠ `new int?()` is refused — there is no operand to leave behind — as is a named argument, an object initializer on the creation, and new(5), which is an ImplicitObjectCreationExpression and not this shape at all: nothing is written there to be redundant. ⚠ Every whitelisted position accepts an arbitrary expression without parentheses, so the fix never adds any; it is exactly two deletions, new int?( and the ), and a comment or directive inside either one withdraws the finding.
